analysis.one_liner: Redirects part of Social Security payroll taxes into personal stock-and-bond accounts while trimming guaranteed benefits and raising the retirement age.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, sent to its Social Security Subcommittee, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let workers divert roughly a fifth of their Social Security payroll taxes into personal retirement accounts invested in stocks and corporate bonds. To pay for it, it would cut guaranteed Social Security benefits, gradually raise the retirement age, and route tens to hundreds of billions of dollars a year from the general Treasury fund into the transition. It also included tax breaks for retirement saving, long-term care insurance, and family caregivers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who join the program would own accounts that could earn higher returns than the current system promises, and would pass any remaining balance to their heirs. Low earners would get a small refundable deposit of $150-$300 a year into their accounts. Investment fund managers would gain a large new stream of mandatory contributions, since account money could only be invested in government-approved mutual funds, and the financial industry would also gain from permanent IRA and pension tax rules and faster increases in contribution limits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Future retirees with accounts, and fund managers

how_it_helps.text: Workers would have Social Security taxes redirected into personal retirement savings accounts they own, with any balance left at death paid to their estate rather than lost [S3].

Accounts would be invested in broad stock indexes and corporate bonds through three fund options (60/40, 40/60, 80/20), with the bill's findings citing roughly 7% historical real stock returns versus 1.5-2% real returns credited to payroll taxes [S3].
Low-income participants would receive a refundable credit of $300 a year (for incomes between $5,000 and $25,000) deposited into their accounts [S3].
The bill would make permanent the pension and IRA provisions of the 2001 tax law and accelerate scheduled increases in IRA and pension contribution limits [S2, S3].

Caregivers would gain: years spent providing child care would be disregarded in benefit calculations, and taxpayers supporting dependent parents in their households or buying long-term care insurance would get new tax credits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers would bear most of the cost: guaranteed benefits would be reduced by an amount tied to the money redirected into accounts, a new benefit formula would phase in cuts of up to 17% for middle and higher earners, the full retirement age would rise beyond 67, and the benefit formula would switch from wage indexing to slower price indexing. The general Treasury fund would cover transition costs of $21 billion in 2007 rising to $283 billion by 2013. Account holders would bear market risk, with withdrawals taxed like Social Security benefits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers through benefit cuts and later retirement

drawbacks.text: Guaranteed benefits would be cut: the primary insurance amount would be reduced by the value of taxes redirected to accounts, and a new benefit formula would impose additional reductions reaching 17% for middle and higher earners by 2018 or later [S3].
The normal retirement age would gradually rise above 67, and the early retirement age would rise as well, meaning people would have to work longer for full benefits [S3].
The benefit formula's bend points would be indexed to consumer prices instead of wages, which slowly shrinks benefits relative to living standards for every future retiree [S3].

Transition costs would be large: the bill itself appropriates $21 billion in fiscal 2007 rising to $283 billion in 2013 from the general fund, on top of the tax revenue diverted from Social Security [S3].

Market risk would shift to workers: accounts could be invested only in government-approved index funds, distributions would be taxed like Social Security benefits, and an individual who opted back into traditional Social Security would have to return the account balance to the trust funds [S3].
The bill directs a study on letting individuals opt out of Social Security coverage entirely, a step that would remove even more revenue from the system [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real ownership and potentially higher retirement income, and its caregiver and low-income provisions were genuinely helpful. But the trade was lopsided: the same bill that created the accounts cut guaranteed benefits by up to 17%, raised the retirement age, and switched benefit growth to a slower index, all to fund the transition. Whether workers came out ahead would depend entirely on market returns over decades, with the investment fund industry collecting fees on every dollar in between. The transition would also add hundreds of billions to federal borrowing during years of large deficits.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, then to the committee's Social Security Subcommittee two weeks later, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Smith (R-MI) introduced the Social Security Solvency Act of 2003 on September 10, 2003, joined by Reps. Kolbe, Stenholm, Toomey, Shadegg, and Flake as original sponsors [S3, S5].
The House referred the bill to the Ways and Means Committee the same day, and on September 30, 2003, referred it to the Subcommittee on Social Security [S5].
The subcommittee took no further action on the bill; the only recorded activity afterward was Smith delivering introductory remarks on the House floor several times, most recently in July 2004 [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People relying on Social Security's guaranteed benefits came out ahead, since nothing changed for them. The investment industry lost the chance at a new stream of managed retirement assets that the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on guaranteed Social Security benefits

sides.party_line_note: Eight of the bill's nine cosponsors were Republicans; the exception was Democrat Charles Stenholm of Texas, one of the House's most conservative Democrats. No votes were ever taken, so the broader chambers never weighed in.

industries.industry: Investment fund and asset management industry
industries.note: The bill would make government-approved mutual funds the mandatory channel for roughly a fifth of workers' Social Security taxes, creating a permanent, fee-earning stream of assets for fund managers. It replaces part of a public program that charges almost nothing with privately managed funds, while the guarantee workers gave up in exchange is cut.

The bill creates a refundable tax credit for premiums on qualified long-term care insurance and revises the requirements for such contracts, subsidizing purchases of a private product with taxpayer money.

industries.industry: Retirement plan and financial services providers
industries.note: The bill makes the 2001 law's IRA and pension provisions permanent and accelerates increases in contribution limits, expanding the tax-advantaged retirement products the industry sells.
